content: The global rates of caesarean section (CS) have been increasing, making it essential to identify and utilize the safest and most effective surgical techniques. This study aimed to compare the outcomes of different complete methods of caesarean section and to summarize findings from reviews of specific aspects of CS techniques. A systematic search was conducted in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register (as of August 2007), the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (Issue 3, 2007), and reference lists of relevant studies. The search was updated on February 15, 2012, with additional results awaiting classification. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared different techniques for performing caesarean sections. Two independent reviewers assessed the studies and extracted data for analysis. The findings revealed that the 'Joel-Cohen based' technique, when compared to the Pfannenstiel method, demonstrated several advantages: 1. Reduced Blood Loss: Women undergoing the Joel-Cohen technique experienced significantly less intraoperative blood loss. Across five trials involving 481 women, the weighted mean difference (WMD) in blood loss was -64.45 mL (95% confidence interval [CI]: -91.34 to -37.56 mL). 2. Shorter Operating Time: The Joel-Cohen method resulted in a shorter duration of surgery. In five trials with 581 women, the WMD for operating time was -18.65 minutes (95% CI: -24.84 to -12.45 minutes). 3. Faster Postoperative Recovery: Women in the Joel-Cohen group had a reduced time to oral intake postoperatively. Data from five trials involving 481 women showed a WMD of -3.92 hours (95% CI: -7.13 to -0.71 hours). 4. Lower Incidence of Postoperative Fever: The risk of developing fever postoperatively was lower with the Joel-Cohen technique. Eight trials with 1,412 women reported a relative risk (RR) of 0.47 (95% CI: 0.28 to 0.81). 5. Shorter Duration of Postoperative Pain: Women experienced less postoperative pain with the Joel-Cohen method. In one trial with two comparisons involving 172 women, the WMD for pain duration was -14.18 hours (95% CI: -18.31 to -10.04 hours). 6. Reduced Need for Analgesic Injections: Fewer analgesic injections were required postoperatively in the Joel-Cohen group. Two trials with 151 women reported a WMD of -0.92 injections (95% CI: -1.20 to -0.63). 7. Quicker Delivery of the Baby: The time from skin incision to the birth of the baby was shorter with the Joel-Cohen technique. Five trials involving 575 women showed a WMD of -3.84 minutes (95% CI: -5.41 to -2.27 minutes). The analysis did not include sufficient data to evaluate serious complications or the need for blood transfusions due to their low incidence in the trials. In conclusion, the 'Joel-Cohen based' technique offers several advantages over the Pfannenstiel and traditional lower midline caesarean section methods. These benefits could potentially lead to cost savings for healthcare systems. However, the trials reviewed did not provide data on mortality or serious long-term complications, such as morbidly adherent placenta or uterine scar rupture. It is also noted that the 19 citations awaiting classification may influence the conclusions of this review once they are assessed.
